neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Speech fluent with normal rate and prosody. No dysarthria or word-finding difficulty. Naming, repetition, and comprehension intact. Recall 3/3 at registration and 3/3 at 5 minutes. Attention intact; serial sevens performed accurately. neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive 3 mm to 2 mm bilaterally. Visual fields full to confrontation. Extraocular movements intact without nystagmus or ptosis. Facial sensation intact in all three divisions bilaterally. Facial symmetry preserved at rest and with activation. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally. Palate elevates symmetrically. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. Tongue midline without atrophy or fasciculations.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Tone normal in upper extremities; no rigidity or spasticity. In the left lower extremity, the patient demonstrates collapsing (give-way) weakness at hip flexion and knee extension, with initial effort appearing 4/5 that suddenly collapses to 1/5 when resistance is applied. Right lower extremity strength 5/5 throughout. Upper extremity strength 5/5 bilaterally. Positive Hoover sign on the left: when testing left hip flexion, involuntary extension is palpable in the contralateral right hip. Intermittent coarse tremor of the left hand noted during examination, variable in amplitude and frequency, which entrains to the frequency of voluntary rhythmic tapping with the right hand and resolves entirely when the patient is asked to perform rapid alternating movements with the right hand.
neurological_exam.sensory: Reports complete loss of sensation to light touch, pinprick, temperature, and vibration in the left leg extending to the inguinal crease with an exact midline split at the abdomen. Proprioception intact bilaterally when tested. Right side sensation fully intact. No extinction on double simultaneous stimulation.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor (downgoing) bilaterally. No clonus.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin on the right performed smoothly. On the left, the patient demonstrates inconsistent performance with large-amplitude wavering that does not follow a cerebellar pattern; performance improves with distraction.
neurological_exam.gait: Patient walks with a markedly antalgic pattern, dragging the left leg with circumduction. However, the pattern is inconsistent: when asked to walk backward, gait normalizes significantly. Tandem gait attempted with dramatic swaying but no falls. Romberg testing shows large-amplitude swaying in all directions that increases with observation but the patient consistently catches herself without falling.
neurological_exam.additional: During the examination, the patient had a witnessed episode lasting approximately 2 minutes characterized by bilateral upper extremity tremor with asynchronous, irregular jerking, eyes tightly closed, and side-to-side head movements. The patient was verbally responsive during the episode, answering her name and following simple commands (e.g., 'squeeze my fingers'). The episode terminated abruptly without post-ictal confusion or drowsiness. Notably, serum sodium was checked and was 131 mEq/L at the time. The examiner observed that the patient's excessive water intake during the admission (estimated 5-6 liters per day) may be contributing to persistent mild hyponatremia.

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive left leg weakness and numbness over 5 weeks, with three episodes of shaking and unresponsiveness over the past 2 weeks
patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Reyes is a 32-year-old right-handed elementary school teacher who presents to the neurology inpatient service following transfer from an outside emergency department after an episode of bilateral shaking with apparent unresponsiveness witnessed by her coworker at school. She reports that the first such episode occurred approximately two weeks ago while she was at home alone. She describes suddenly feeling overwhelmed, followed by trembling in both arms that progressed to whole-body shaking lasting approximately one to two minutes. She states that she could hear her surroundings throughout the event but felt unable to move or speak. There was no tongue biting, urinary incontinence, or injury. She recovered rapidly without confusion. A second episode occurred one week later at a grocery store, witnessed by bystanders who called emergency services. She was taken to a local emergency department where a CT head was reported as normal, basic labs were drawn showing a serum sodium of 129 mEq/L, and she was discharged with a recommendation for outpatient neurology follow-up.

The third and most recent episode occurred yesterday at her workplace. A coworker described bilateral arm shaking and apparent unresponsiveness lasting approximately 90 seconds, during which the patient's eyes were tightly closed. The coworker reported that the patient seemed to respond to her name being called by squeezing her hand. No tonic posturing, cyanosis, or incontinence was noted. Emergency medical services were called and the patient was brought to the emergency department and subsequently admitted.

In addition to these episodic events, Ms. Reyes reports progressive weakness in her left leg that began approximately five weeks ago. She initially noticed difficulty going up stairs, and the weakness has worsened to the point where she now drags her left foot while walking. She also describes complete numbness of the left leg from the hip down, stating she cannot feel anything when she touches it. She denies any back pain, trauma, bowel or bladder dysfunction, or recent infections. She reports that the weakness fluctuates somewhat throughout the day and seems worse when she is under stress.

The patient has a notable medical history of psychogenic polydipsia diagnosed four years ago after evaluation for recurrent hyponatremia. She reports that she continues to drink large quantities of water daily, often 4 to 6 liters, describing an intense compulsion to drink that worsens with anxiety. Her most recent hospitalization for hyponatremia was eight months ago. She acknowledges significant recent psychosocial stressors, including separation from her partner of six years two months ago and increasing workplace demands that have left her feeling overwhelmed. She has been on medical leave for three weeks due to her neurological symptoms. Her grandmother had epilepsy, which has heightened her fear that she may also have epilepsy. She has been reading about seizure disorders online and is convinced she has developed the same condition. She reports poor sleep with frequent awakenings, decreased appetite, and a 4 kg weight loss over the past two months.

clinical_assessment.impression: Positive functional signs elicited and documented: Collapsing (give-way) weakness, Hoover sign, Tremor entrainment test, Midline-splitting sensory loss, Internal inconsistency on repeat testing, Improvement with attentional distraction, Dragging monoplegic gait. Functional neurological disorder is a rule-in diagnosis under DSM-5 and the criterion satisfied here is clinical incompatibility, not the absence of another disease. No further investigation is required to make the diagnosis; whatever imaging or laboratory testing is performed is for a separate, specific question.

results.title: Psychogenic polydipsia and functional neurological disorder: shared mechanisms of somatization
results.journal: Journal of Neurology Neurosurgery and Psychiatry
results.summary: Both psychogenic polydipsia and FND can be conceptualized within a framework of altered interoceptive processing, where internal bodily signals are misinterpreted or amplified. Shared psychiatric comorbidities (anxiety, depression, trauma history) are common.

results.title: Diagnosis and management of functional neurological disorder
results.authors: Espay AJ, Aybek S, Carson A et al.
results.summary: FND should be diagnosed by positive clinical signs (Hoover sign, tremor entrainment, etc.), not by exclusion. A multidisciplinary approach combining neurology, psychiatry, physiotherapy, and psychology is recommended.

results.title: Hyponatremia and seizures: distinguishing organic from functional etiologies
results.summary: Hyponatremia below 120 mEq/L can provoke true epileptic seizures. Mild hyponatremia (130-135 mEq/L) is unlikely to cause seizures in isolation but may lower seizure threshold. In patients with PNES, coexisting mild hyponatremia should not lead to misdiagnosis of epileptic seizures.

output.summary: Psychogenic polydipsia and FND share underlying mechanisms related to altered interoceptive processing and somatization, and frequently co-occur with anxiety, depression, and trauma history. Mild hyponatremia from polydipsia (>125 mEq/L) is unlikely to cause true epileptic seizures but is a recognised diagnostic confounder in patients with episodic neurological events. FND diagnosis relies on positive clinical signs rather than exclusion of organic disease.

specialized_test.impression: The study was performed and is normal. It does not contribute to the diagnosis in this presentation, and the negative result is itself a harm in a functional disorder: it reinforces the search for an organic cause the positive signs have already answered.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion disorder) with mixed symptoms — psychogenic non-epileptic seizures and functional limb weakness, comorbid with psychogenic polydipsia

differential.key_features: Witnessed convulsive-appearing events; ictal video-EEG showing absence of electrographic correlate during a captured habitual event is the key differentiator.
Sensorimotor symptoms in a young adult raise demyelinating disease; brain (and when indicated spine) MRI without T2/FLAIR lesions or enhancement argues against an active demyelinating process.
Focal complaints warrant imaging; normal brain MRI without lesion, mass, or enhancement effectively excludes a structural cause for the presenting deficit.
Non-dermatomal sensory loss, normal reflexes, and (when obtained) normal EMG/NCS argue against peripheral nerve or root pathology.
Episodic neurological symptoms can occur in autoimmune encephalitis; normal MRI, normal EEG background, and (when obtained) negative antibody panel render this very unlikely.

FND is involuntary; preserved effort on symptom-validity testing and absence of clear secondary gain argue against feigning. The rule-in signs do not distinguish FND from malingering by themselves, but the clinical context does not support a feigning explanation.

useless_tools.rationale: Echocardiography has no role in FND; no structural cardiac question is raised by the presentation.
Cardiac rhythm monitoring is not indicated; the events are non-syncopal and the rule-in signs point to FND.
Non-contrast head CT adds no information beyond MRI for an FND workup and contributes diagnostic noise plus radiation exposure.
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in typical FND; invasive testing reinforces somatic illness model and adds iatrogenic risk without changing management.
Advanced PET imaging has no indication in FND; standard MRI is the appropriate structural workup.

Nerve conduction studies and EMG have no role once positive functional signs are documented: the deficit is not neuromuscular, the study is uncomfortable, and a normal result reinforces the patient's search for an organic cause — the principal iatrogenic harm in this condition
Somatosensory evoked potentials answer a question about a lesion in the somatosensory pathway; a midline-splitting, non-anatomical sensory deficit is not that question

critical_actions: Do NOT make the diagnosis by exclusion: document at least one positive rule-in sign, which is the act that establishes it
Obtain video-EEG capturing a habitual event with normal interictal EEG to confirm PNES
Communicate the diagnosis transparently using positive language and the rule-in signs as the basis
Refer for FND-informed physiotherapy and CBT / psychological therapy
Order a comprehensive neuropsychological battery to characterize comorbid depression, anxiety, somatization, and trauma exposure — informs treatment planning (criteria-pack 'recommended' tier)

Communicate the diagnosis transparently using positive language anchored on the rule-in signs; explicitly state the diagnosis is FND, the symptoms are real and involuntary, and there is an evidence-based treatment plan
Refer to specialized FND-informed physiotherapy (for functional motor symptoms) and to CBT / psychological therapy (for PNES and comorbid mood / anxiety)
contraindicated_actions: Do not pursue ever-expanding negative investigations — per Stone 2018, repeated negative workups reinforce illness conviction and worsen prognosis
Do not frame the diagnosis as 'all in your head', 'nothing wrong', or 'we couldn't find anything' — this damages the therapeutic alliance and is the most common avoidable harm in FND
Do not perform invasive testing (lumbar puncture, nerve biopsy, muscle biopsy, cerebral angiography) when positive rule-in signs are present and there is no clinical indication
Do not order EMG/NCS, muscle biopsy, or nerve biopsy as part of an FND workup — these invasive tests reinforce the somatic illness model per Stone 2018
Do not start or continue long-term anti-epileptic drugs for functional (psychogenic non-epileptic) seizures — AEDs are ineffective for PNES and expose the patient to side effects
Do not give benzodiazepines as abortive therapy for witnessed PNES events (no benefit and risk of respiratory depression)
Do not give gadolinium without a specific indication — contrast adds cost and risk and answers no question that positive functional signs have not already answered

Do not repeat the brain MRI, the laboratory panel or the lumbar puncture once a first normal study and positive rule-in signs are documented: each repetition strengthens the patient's belief that something organic has been missed
key_reasoning_points: FND is a positive diagnosis based on rule-in signs (Hoover, tremor entrainment, give-way weakness, non-dermatomal sensory loss with midline split) — not a diagnosis of exclusion (Espay 2018, Stone 2018).

Brain MRI and basic laboratory testing are OPTIONAL here, not due diligence: the diagnosis rests on the positive signs, and each additional negative study is a cost and an iatrogenic harm rather than a confirmation. Where imaging is recommended in this case it is for one specific alternative question, once.
Over-investigation is the principal iatrogenic harm in FND; every additional negative test reinforces the patient's illness conviction and worsens prognosis (Stone 2018).
Psychiatric comorbidity (anxiety, depression, trauma) is common and informs treatment planning but is NOT required for the diagnosis and does not 'explain' the symptoms in a reductive sense.
Diagnostic communication matters: using positive language anchored on the rule-in signs is associated with better engagement and outcomes (Stone 2018).
Evidence-based treatment is multidisciplinary — CBT for PNES and FND-informed physiotherapy for functional motor symptoms (Nielsen 2015).
Video-EEG capturing a habitual event with normal interictal EEG is diagnostic for PNES (ILAE PNES Task Force 2013); routine EEG alone is insufficient.

Interim composition decision, August 2026: FND remains only to keep the frozen dataset at 20 conditions/600 cases. The positive functional-neurological examination is the sole required diagnostic act; every instrumental test is optional and case-targeted. DLB remains the preferred future replacement when composition work resumes.

red_herrings.data_point: Family history of multiple sclerosis in a relative
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on a demyelinating diagnosis (MS) and pursue extensive MS-specific workup before considering FND
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Non-first-degree family history of MS is a weak risk factor; the patient's symptoms must be evaluated on positive findings. Normal brain MRI without demyelinating lesions effectively addresses this concern.

red_herrings.data_point: Family history of epilepsy in a relative
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on an epileptic etiology and pursue prolonged AED trials before confirming PNES with video-EEG
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Family history of epilepsy does not establish the patient's events as epileptic. Video-EEG capturing the habitual event without ictal correlate is the gold standard.

red_herrings.data_point: Pre-existing psychiatric diagnosis (anxiety or depression) in the past medical history
red_herrings.intended_effect: Premature anchoring on a 'psychosomatic' label without obtaining positive rule-in signs; conversely, dismissing FND as a serious diagnosis because the patient is 'just anxious'
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Psychiatric comorbidity neither establishes nor refutes FND. Diagnosis requires positive rule-in signs on examination; psychiatric history is relevant for treatment planning, not for diagnosis.

red_herrings.data_point: Reported history of psychological trauma or recent stressor
red_herrings.intended_effect: Use trauma history to make FND a 'foregone conclusion' without verifying positive rule-in signs
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Trauma is enriched in FND populations (Stone 2018) but is neither necessary nor sufficient for diagnosis. Positive rule-in signs remain the diagnostic anchor.

metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate difficulty due to the diagnostic confounder of coexisting psychogenic polydipsia with mild hyponatremia, which could be misattributed as the cause of seizure-like episodes. Family history of epilepsy adds further misdirection. The agent must correctly identify that the hyponatremia is too mild to cause seizures and recognize the positive functional signs pointing to FND/PNES.
clinical_pearls: Psychogenic polydipsia and FND share underlying mechanisms of somatization and altered interoceptive processing
Hyponatremia below 120 mEq/L can cause seizures; levels of 130-135 mEq/L are unlikely to provoke epileptic activity
Maximally dilute urine in the setting of hyponatremia indicates appropriate renal response to excess water, confirming primary polydipsia and excluding SIADH
Hoover sign: involuntary hip extension on the contralateral side when testing hip flexion — a reliable positive sign of functional weakness
Tremor entrainment: functional tremor changes frequency to match voluntary rhythmic movements of another limb
Tight eye closure during seizure-like events is more common in PNES than epileptic seizures
Midline splitting of sensory loss is a positive functional sign, as true spinal or peripheral lesions do not produce exact midline split
metadata.revision_reason: FND interim reviewer option: positive clinical diagnosis required; every instrumental test optional and selected for explicit red flags
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Mixed motor and/or seizure phenotype with at least one prominent comorbidity or compelling red herring (family history of MS, antipsychotic exposure, comorbid SLE). Standard FND workup (MRI + basic labs + video-EEG when seizure phenotype) plus disciplined diagnostic communication.
